correctness.rationale: The planar geometric reduction is sound. For a strictly convex compact unit ball and a nonzero translation, horizontal cross-sections have a concave width function; more than two common boundary points at one translation length would force a nontrivial constant-width level segment and hence affine boundary arcs, contradicting strict convexity. Thus a unit pair with a fixed nonzero sum has at most the two ordered endpoints of one chord. For any four unit vectors summing to zero, the first pair and negatives of the second pair share the same sum, so the four points must form two antipodal pairs; the zero pair-sum and repeated-point cases are separately covered. For an antipodal quadruple the sum of all six squared pairwise distances is exactly eight plus twice the two modified von Neumann–Jordan numerator terms, so taking the supremum gives the stated identity. The endpoint normed-plane examples and the published universal upper bound supply the non-strictly-convex endpoint values, while the cited exact modified von Neumann–Jordan constant supplies the interior finite-dimensional profile.

originality.rationale: The defining inscribed-quadrilateral paper was inspected and gives the general lower bound of eight times the modified von Neumann–Jordan constant plus eight, along with universal bounds and polygonal examples, but it does not identify strictly convex normed planes as an equality class. The Ciesielski--Płuciennik paper computes modified von Neumann–Jordan constants but does not address the four-point inscribed-quadrilateral invariant. The submitted theorem's nontrivial step is the planar strict-convexity collapse of every centered inscribed quadruple to two antipodal pairs; no checked source stated that reduction or the resulting exact identity.

value.rationale: The theorem upgrades a published general lower bound to an exact identity on the natural class of strictly convex normed planes and turns a four-point optimization into a classical two-point invariant. That reduction yields a complete exact profile for the standard two-dimensional ell-p family and exposes a genuinely planar structural phenomenon that fails in higher dimension.

limitations: The structural identity is restricted to real two-dimensional strictly convex normed spaces.
The non-strict ell-one and ell-infinity endpoint values are handled separately and do not follow from the strict-convexity collapse.
